The Week the Guardrails Were Tested

Mass firings, a corruption case dropped, and a president who says courts don't bind him

```markdown This was a week in which nearly every check on executive power was tested at once, and in most cases the executive did not yield. A corruption case against a sitting mayor collapsed under apparent political pressure, a new cost-cutting body pushed into the government's most sensitive data systems, courts issued rulings the administration sometimes ignored, and a state governor's public refusal to comply with a presidential directive brought immediate federal retaliation. By week's end, the country's institutional guardrails had been pushed in nearly every direction, with mixed and often unresolved results.

The week began over the weekend with an eruption inside the Justice Department. Acting US attorneys and senior officials in the Southern District of New York and the Public Integrity Section resigned rather than carry out an order to drop corruption charges against New York Mayor Eric Adams, a case critics said was being traded away in exchange for Adams' cooperation on immigration enforcement. The resignations were the opening move in what would become a running story through the middle of the week. Alongside the Adams fallout, Trump signed executive orders empowering the newly formed DOGE committee, led by Elon Musk, to shrink the federal workforce, and ended COVID-19 vaccine mandates in schools by threatening to withhold federal education funding. The administration also faced accusations of ignoring court orders altogether, including a pause on USAID staff leave that employees said was disregarded when they were turned away from their offices anyway. Elsewhere, DOJ fired more than two dozen immigration judges even as 3.5 million cases sat backlogged, the Associated Press was barred from White House coverage over its refusal to rename the Gulf of Mexico, and workforce cuts hit the Forest Service, Park Service, USDA's animal disease lab network, and the CFPB.

By Monday, the Adams case moved a step closer to resolution as the Justice Department formally requested dismissal of the charges, and another senior DOJ official, Denise Cheung, resigned rather than follow a directive she considered unethical. The same day, the IRS began reviewing a request to give DOGE personnel access to classified taxpayer records, prompting a lawsuit from 19 state attorneys general over similar access sought at Treasury. Courts, meanwhile, issued a mixed batch of rulings on emergency motions tied to DOGE and personnel actions, including continuing uncertainty over the fate of Special Counsel Hampton Dellinger, whose removal was headed toward the Supreme Court.

Tuesday brought one of the week's most consequential single actions: an executive order asserting direct presidential control over independent regulatory agencies including the SEC and FTC, requiring them to submit proposed rules for White House review and declaring the president's and attorney general's legal interpretations controlling across the executive branch. That same day, the Justice Department formally dismissed the corruption case against Adams, closing the loop that had begun with weekend resignations and confirming, for many observers, that prosecutorial power had been used as political leverage. On a separate but related front, twenty-two red states and oil industry groups sued to block climate superfund laws in New York and Vermont, while the federal solicitor general opposed reviving the youth-led Juliana climate case — a coordinated legal push against state-level climate accountability efforts. Courts also issued a dense batch of rulings on pending motions touching DOGE, agency firings, and diversity-related orders, granting some relief and denying other requests, underscoring how much of the week's activity remained legally contested.

Wednesday was the busiest day of the week by a wide margin. Trump signed an executive order attempting to reinterpret the 14th Amendment to deny automatic citizenship to children born to parents without permanent legal status — a move estimated to affect roughly 255,000 births annually — only to have a federal appeals court deny the administration's request to reinstate the policy. The same day, DOGE was formally established by executive order with Musk named to lead it, even as later court filings would claim he held no formal decision-making authority within it. A cluster of additional orders restricted undocumented immigrants' access to federal benefits, directed agencies to review and potentially rescind regulations deemed unconstitutional, and eliminated several federal entities and advisory committees. In the Adams matter, acting deputy attorney general Emil Bove appeared before a Manhattan judge to defend the dismissal, arguing that continued prosecution would impede Adams' cooperation with immigration enforcement; the judge questioned the rationale sharply without ruling. On foreign policy, following a call with Vladimir Putin, Trump publicly blamed Ukraine for the ongoing war and suggested President Zelensky should hold elections — language that echoed demands long made by Moscow. Federal websites also saw references to Black Americans removed during Black History Month, and the National Park Service stripped references to transgender people from its pages. Separately, a federal judge allowed the administration's mass firings of federal workers to continue, rejecting a union bid to halt them, even as another judge questioned whether the DOJ itself understood the scope of its own personnel actions.

Thursday's developments centered on two parallel institutional tests. Courts intervened repeatedly against DOGE's expanding data access: lawsuits sought to block the group from Department of Labor, Education, and Treasury systems, and federal judges restricted DOGE's access to Treasury data to two vetted staffers, one of whom resigned after past racist posts surfaced. At the same time, the Senate confirmed Kash Patel as FBI director in a narrow 51-49 vote, installing an election denier and Trump loyalist who has spoken of targeting "deep state" officials and media organizations atop federal law enforcement. The Justice Department also declared job protections for administrative law judges unconstitutional, moving to bring them under more direct presidential control, extending the week's broader pattern of subordinating independent adjudicative bodies. In a separate move, the US Marshals Service was ordered to deputize Musk's private security detail, granting armed authority on federal property without standard vetting. The administration also directed New York City to end congestion pricing and froze congressionally approved EV subsidies. Away from the executive branch, Mitch McConnell announced he would not seek re-election in 2026, and Senator Angus King warned that the administration's impoundment actions represented the most serious constitutional assault in the country's history.

The week closed on Friday with its sharpest confrontation between federal and state power. At a White House meeting, Trump told Maine Governor Janet Mills to comply with his ban on transgender athletes in girls' sports or lose federal funding, declaring "we are the federal law." Mills responded, "see you in court." Within hours, multiple federal agencies opened investigations into Maine's policies — a rapid sequence that made explicit how quickly institutional defiance could draw federal retaliation. The same day, Trump fired Gen. CQ Brown Jr., chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, along with the Navy chief, the Air Force vice chief, and senior military lawyers, reportedly over their resistance to diversity policies — a sweeping removal of military leadership that raised concerns about the politicization of the armed forces. A federal judge in Maryland separately blocked enforcement of the administration's anti-DEI directives as likely unconstitutional, finding they probably violated the First Amendment. Labor unions filed suit alleging DOGE had unlawfully accessed Social Security data, extending the week's pattern of legal challenges to the group's reach. Elsewhere, a judge cleared the way for more than 2,000 USAID workers to be placed on leave while the Forest Service and Interior Department continued firing probationary employees, and the SEC agreed to drop its enforcement lawsuit against Coinbase without penalty as Attorney General Pam Bondi told Fox News that Jeffrey Epstein case files were "sitting on my desk." The week's final loose thread involved January 6 defendants: several pardoned participants, including Enrique Tarrio, announced a lawsuit against the Justice Department over their original prosecutions, even as Tarrio was arrested near the Capitol days later for allegedly assaulting a protester.

Taken as a whole, the week showed executive power probing nearly every seam in the system built to constrain it — prosecutorial independence, regulatory autonomy, judicial protections, military leadership, press access, and constitutional citizenship guarantees among them. Courts intervened repeatedly, sometimes decisively, as with the birthright citizenship rebuff and the DEI injunction, and sometimes only partially, as with the piecemeal restrictions on DOGE's data access. Career officials resigned rather than comply with directives they viewed as improper, while a state governor chose public defiance over compliance and drew immediate federal scrutiny in return. None of these confrontations reached final resolution by Friday; instead, the week left behind a docket of unresolved lawsuits, pending appeals, and open investigations that will shape how much of this contested authority ultimately survives legal and institutional review. ```
